PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

# Proposition 42: Ban new taxes on personal property
## What does California Proposition 42 do?
Proposition 42 would make it much harder to create a wealth tax in California by prohibiting new taxes on the mere ownership of assets such as investment accounts, business interests and personal property — assets that are typically only taxed when they are sold or generate income.
Like Proposition 41, which also attempts to block Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 42 would nullify Proposition 40 if it receives more votes, even if the billionaire tax also passes.
It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. Citrin-POLITICO Oct 19 poll: need Prop 42 numbers.

The key methodological difference: PPIC uses a probability-based panel (Ipsos KnowledgePanel) with low undecided rates (2-4%) — respondents are forced to choose. IGS's online poll has large undecided (12-23%).

Which is more predictive? PPIC has historically been one of the better California ballot measure pollsters. IGS has had mixed accuracy. Note: IGS's high undecided rates mean their yes/no split among decided voters: Oct: 43/(43+45) = 48.9% yes. Sept: 43/77 = 53.2%. Aug: 40/77 = 51.9%.

PPIC Oct: 51/(51+47) = 52.0% yes. Sept: 54/97 = 55.7%.

So among decided voters, IGS Oct shows 48.9% yes — just below half. PPIC shows 52% yes.

Hmm, both show decline. The average of the last two polls among decided voters: ~50.5%. That's essentially a coin flip.

Key additional considerations:

1. **Undecided resolution**: In IGS, undecided fell from 23% to 12%. If undecided break mostly against (which is what happened between Sept and Oct: no rose from 34 to 45, yes flat at 43), that suggests a trend unfavorable to Yes.

2. **Late-campaign momentum**: Both polls show decline in support for Prop 42. The "billionaire-funded trick" message is landing. LA Times quote from DiCamillo: "it's moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a lat[e campaign]..." — implying measures moving down late tend to lose.

3. **Money**: Yes on 42 has $157M vs No $34.5M. That's a huge advantage — 4.5:1. And the "Yes" side is running ads about protecting retirement savings. Historically, heavy spending advantage correlates with wins, though not deterministically.

4. **Newsom endorsement**: Oct 9. Newsom is popular in CA. That helps Yes.

5. **Ballot fatigue / confusion**: 14 propositions; voters find the language complicated. When confused, voters tend to vote "no" (status quo bias). PPIC found likely voters agree that the wording for citizens' initiatives is too complicated. That's a headwind for Prop 42 — a technical, hard-to-understand measure.

Actually wait — but the title "Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes" is quite comprehensible as an anti-tax measure, and anti-tax measures generally poll well.

6. **Base rates**: California citizen initiatives pass at a low rate. Actually 2024 CA had Props 2-36, many legislatively referred. Citizen initiatives in 2024: 4 (yes), 5 (no), 6 (no), 9 (no), 10 (no)... Let me not go down this path too far. Roughly, about 40-50% of citizen initiatives pass in CA in the last decade when well-funded.

Hmm. Let me think about the "two measures competing" dynamic. There's an important subtlety: Some voters who support Prop 40 (billionaire tax) might still vote yes on Prop 42 because they like the "protect retirement savings" framing. And indeed PPIC shows Prop 42 (51%) outpolling Prop 40 (46%). IGS shows Prop 42 (43%) basically tied with Prop 40 (42%).

Proposition 42 : Ban new state taxes on personal property
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 42 would bar any new state tax on owning financial assets or other personal property, meaning everything people own other than real estate. It would also limit new state taxes that apply retroactively to things that happened before the tax took effect. It applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, and would cancel conflicting taxes enacted after that date. If it gets more yes votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 42
New state taxes it bars Taxes on owning personal property (retirement accounts, stocks, business interests, art and other non-real-estate assets), and most retroactive taxes, if enacted from Jan. 1, 2026
Taxes it leaves alone Real property taxes, and any tax in effect and first collected by Dec. 31, 2025
Effect on Proposition 40 If 42 gets more yes votes than 40, 40 could be stopped (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, 2026 through Nov. 1 For: $159.28 million, almost all from Building a Better California. Against: no committee formed only against 42; a combined Yes on 40, No on 41 and 42 committee raised $32.89 million through Nov. 1
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 51% yes, 47% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 43% yes, 45% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures come from the committees' state campaign statements and late contribution reports (Cal-Access).
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 42 mean?
The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
What does a no vote on Proposition 42 mean?
The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
What would Proposition 42 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the state would have fewer options for raising taxes, so future tax revenue could be lower than it otherwise would be. When and by how much is unclear.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 42 limits new state taxes. It does not change real property taxes or personal property taxes already collected before 2026, such as the business equipment tax counties collect. It does not affect the City's Measure FD or Measure ULA. Its largest effect on this ballot is on Proposition 40: if 42 gets more yes votes, the billionaire tax for health care could be stopped. The Legislative Analyst does not estimate effects on the City of Los Angeles.
The details
Official title Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
What would change
Today If Proposition 42 passes
Taxes on owning personal property The state and local governments tax some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee and the property tax on business equipment paid to counties. Owning financial assets such as stocks and investment accounts is not taxed (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)) No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026 may impose or authorize a tax “on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
What counts as covered property Not applicable Pensions, 401(k), 403(b) and other retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all personal property, tangible or intangible, including financial assets, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Retroactive taxes Allowed in some cases. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)) Barred for taxes based on conduct, activities or a status before the tax took effect, including residency on an earlier date. The Legislature may reach back up to 365 days only for a declared emergency or fiscal emergency, with the money limited to that emergency (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Existing taxes In effect Not affected if in effect and first collected by Dec. 31, 2025 (text, Art. VIII, Secs. 1(b) and 2(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Real property (land and buildings) Taxed under Proposition 13 rules No change (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The measure adds a new Article VIII to the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst says it “restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future,” which “could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear” (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)).
How it interacts with Proposition 40
Proposition 40 would tax billionaires’ net worth, including businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property, based on residency on Jan. 1, 2026 (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/analysis.htm); official title and summary, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/title-summary.htm)). Proposition 42 bars new taxes on owning those assets and taxes based on residency “on a date prior to the effective date of the tax” (text, Art. VIII, Secs. 1 and 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
The Legislative Analyst: “If Proposition 42 receives more ‘yes’ votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters” (printable guide, Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf)).
Proposition 42’s conflict clause: a measure on the same ballot that taxes ownership of the covered property, or taxes past conduct or status, is “deemed to be in conflict.” If 42 gets more yes votes, “all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void” (text, Sec. 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Proposition 40’s conflict clause: if 40 gets more yes votes than a measure that affects a tax on billionaire net worth, 40’s provisions prevail (text of Proposition 40, Sec. 8 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
The State Constitution: when measures approved at the same election conflict, the one with the most yes votes prevails (Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Tax attorney Megan Jones of Holland & Knight told CalMatters that “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal” than Proposition 41, and that if it passes it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again (LAist via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-could-be-defeated-by-two-other-tax-measures/ar-AA2cUG36)). Proposition 41 is a second measure that could stop Proposition 40 (our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41)). See also our Proposition 40 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-40).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City and County taxes now. Existing local personal property taxes, such as the property tax on business equipment paid to the County, were in effect before 2026 and are not changed (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm); text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Real property taxes and the City’s Measure ULA transfer tax on real estate sales are outside the measure (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Measure FD, a sales tax, is not a tax on owning property.
Future local taxes. The text bars any “state law” enacted from 2026 on that would “authorize collection” of a tax on owning personal property (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). The Attorney General’s summary says it “Prohibits new state taxes on personal property” (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/title-summary.htm)). The Legislative Analyst’s fiscal estimate covers the state’s options to raise taxes and does not discuss new local taxes (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 40 money. Proposition 40 would send 90% of its revenue to health care, mostly state programs such as Medi-Cal (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/analysis.htm)). If Proposition 42 stops it, that money would not be collected. Neither analysis estimates what would reach Los Angeles.
Local money from the Yes campaign. The Yes on 42 committee gave $50,000 on April 13, 2026 to the committee backing the City’s Measure FD, and $10,000 on May 5 to the Los Angeles County Democratic Party’s state candidate committee (Cal-Access, committee 1488418 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1488418); our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd)).
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 42 is a citizen initiative, number 2018 on the Secretary of State’s list (Attorney General file 25-0041A1). The proponent is Kurt R. Oneto, who is also the proponent of Propositions 41 and 45 (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Feb. 11, 2026: The Attorney General issued the circulating title and summary, the same day as Proposition 41 (Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
March 20, 2026: Backers reported 25% of the 874,641 valid signatures needed (Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
June 24, 2026: It became eligible, a week after Proposition 40 (Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Building a Better California, funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other investors, designed Propositions 41 and 42 as countermeasures to Proposition 40, CalMatters reported (LAist via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-could-be-defeated-by-two-other-tax-measures/ar-AA2cUG36)). The Yes committee’s largest payees were PCI Campaigns ($48,791,138) and Amplified Strategies ($7,581,228) (Cal-Access, committee 1488418 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1488418)).
Past wealth tax proposals. Assembly bills to tax the wealth of very rich Californians were introduced in 2020 (AB 2088), 2022 (AB 2289) and 2023 (AB 259). AB 259 died in the Assembly Revenue and Taxation Committee in January 2024; the other two left committee without further action (AB 2088 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB2088); AB 2289 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB2289); AB 259 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB259)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments and rebuttals (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument for, signed by Michael Hedges (California Small Business Association), Shelley Huff (AMVETS, Department of California) and Jennifer Yoder (California Senior Alliance) (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
The Constitution “currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts,” which the authors call “double taxation.”
“In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.”
It “Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts” and “Prohibits retroactive taxes.”
Quotes Chris Hannan, president of the State Building and Construction Trades Council.
The rebuttal, signed by Suzanne Jimenez of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, says it is “a redundant, expensive trick” and that Proposition 40 “ONLY applies to billionaires” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Suzanne Jimenez (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It was “designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.”

Proposition 42 : Ban new state taxes on personal property
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 42 would bar any new state tax on owning financial assets or other personal property, meaning everything people own other than real estate. It would also limit new state taxes that apply retroactively to things that happened before the tax took effect. It applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, and would cancel conflicting taxes enacted after that date. If it gets more yes votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 42
New state taxes it bars Taxes on owning personal property (retirement accounts, stocks, business interests, art and other non-real-estate assets), and most retroactive taxes, if enacted from Jan. 1, 2026
Taxes it leaves alone Real property taxes, and any tax in effect and first collected by Dec. 31, 2025
Effect on Proposition 40 If 42 gets more yes votes than 40, 40 could be stopped (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, 2026 through Nov. 1 For: $159.28 million, almost all from Building a Better California. Against: no committee formed only against 42; a combined Yes on 40, No on 41 and 42 committee raised $32.89 million through Nov. 1
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 51% yes, 47% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 43% yes, 45% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures come from the committees' state campaign statements and late contribution reports (Cal-Access).
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 42 mean?
The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
What does a no vote on Proposition 42 mean?
The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
What would Proposition 42 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the state would have fewer options for raising taxes, so future tax revenue could be lower than it otherwise would be. When and by how much is unclear.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 42 limits new state taxes. It does not change real property taxes or personal property taxes already collected before 2026, such as the business equipment tax counties collect. It does not affect the City's Measure FD or Measure ULA. Its largest effect on this ballot is on Proposition 40: if 42 gets more yes votes, the billionaire tax for health care could be stopped. The Legislative Analyst does not estimate effects on the City of Los Angeles.
The details
Official title Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
What would change
Today If Proposition 42 passes
Taxes on owning personal property The state and local governments tax some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee and the property tax on business equipment paid to counties. Owning financial assets such as stocks and investment accounts is not taxed (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)) No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026 may impose or authorize a tax “on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
What counts as covered property Not applicable Pensions, 401(k), 403(b) and other retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all personal property, tangible or intangible, including financial assets, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Retroactive taxes Allowed in some cases. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)) Barred for taxes based on conduct, activities or a status before the tax took effect, including residency on an earlier date. The Legislature may reach back up to 365 days only for a declared emergency or fiscal emergency, with the money limited to that emergency (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Existing taxes In effect Not affected if in effect and first collected by Dec. 31, 2025 (text, Art. VIII, Secs. 1(b) and 2(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Real property (land and buildings) Taxed under Proposition 13 rules No change (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The measure adds a new Article VIII to the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst says it “restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future,” which “could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear” (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)).
How it interacts with Proposition 40
Proposition 40 would tax billionaires’ net worth, including businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property, based on residency on Jan. 1, 2026 (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/analysis.htm); official title and summary, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/title-summary.htm)). Proposition 42 bars new taxes on owning those assets and taxes based on residency “on a date prior to the effective date of the tax” (text, Art. VIII, Secs. 1 and 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
The Legislative Analyst: “If Proposition 42 receives more ‘yes’ votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters” (printable guide, Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf)).
Proposition 42’s conflict clause: a measure on the same ballot that taxes ownership of the covered property, or taxes past conduct or status, is “deemed to be in conflict.” If 42 gets more yes votes, “all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void” (text, Sec. 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Proposition 40’s conflict clause: if 40 gets more yes votes than a measure that affects a tax on billionaire net worth, 40’s provisions prevail (text of Proposition 40, Sec. 8 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
The State Constitution: when measures approved at the same election conflict, the one with the most yes votes prevails (Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Tax attorney Megan Jones of Holland & Knight told CalMatters that “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal” than Proposition 41, and that if it passes it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again (LAist via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-could-be-defeated-by-two-other-tax-measures/ar-AA2cUG36)). Proposition 41 is a second measure that could stop Proposition 40 (our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41)). See also our Proposition 40 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-40).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City and County taxes now. Existing local personal property taxes, such as the property tax on business equipment paid to the County, were in effect before 2026 and are not changed (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm); text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Real property taxes and the City’s Measure ULA transfer tax on real estate sales are outside the measure (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Measure FD, a sales tax, is not a tax on owning property.
Future local taxes. The text bars any “state law” enacted from 2026 on that would “authorize collection” of a tax on owning personal property (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). The Attorney General’s summary says it “Prohibits new state taxes on personal property” (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/title-summary.htm)). The Legislative Analyst’s fiscal estimate covers the state’s options to raise taxes and does not discuss new local taxes (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 40 money. Proposition 40 would send 90% of its revenue to health care, mostly state programs such as Medi-Cal (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/analysis.htm)). If Proposition 42 stops it, that money would not be collected. Neither analysis estimates what would reach Los Angeles.
Local money from the Yes campaign. The Yes on 42 committee gave $50,000 on April 13, 2026 to the committee backing the City’s Measure FD, and $10,000 on May 5 to the Los Angeles County Democratic Party’s state candidate committee (Cal-Access, committee 1488418 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1488418); our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd)).
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 42 is a citizen initiative, number 2018 on the Secretary of State’s list (Attorney General file 25-0041A1). The proponent is Kurt R. Oneto, who is also the proponent of Propositions 41 and 45 (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Feb. 11, 2026: The Attorney General issued the circulating title and summary, the same day as Proposition 41 (Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
March 20, 2026: Backers reported 25% of the 874,641 valid signatures needed (Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
June 24, 2026: It became eligible, a week after Proposition 40 (Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).

Proposition 42 : Ban new state taxes on personal property
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 42 would bar any new state tax on owning financial assets or other personal property, meaning everything people own other than real estate. It would also limit new state taxes that apply retroactively to things that happened before the tax took effect. It applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, and would cancel conflicting taxes enacted after that date. If it gets more yes votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 42
New state taxes it bars Taxes on owning personal property (retirement accounts, stocks, business interests, art and other non-real-estate assets), and most retroactive taxes, if enacted from Jan. 1, 2026
Taxes it leaves alone Real property taxes, and any tax in effect and first collected by Dec. 31, 2025
Effect on Proposition 40 If 42 gets more yes votes than 40, 40 could be stopped (Legislative Analyst)
Money raised, 2026 through Nov. 1 For: $159.28 million, almost all from Building a Better California. Against: no committee formed only against 42; a combined Yes on 40, No on 41 and 42 committee raised $32.89 million through Nov. 1
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 51% yes, 47% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 43% yes, 45% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures come from the committees' state campaign statements and late contribution reports (Cal-Access).
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 42 mean?
The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
What does a no vote on Proposition 42 mean?
The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
What would Proposition 42 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the state would have fewer options for raising taxes, so future tax revenue could be lower than it otherwise would be. When and by how much is unclear.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 42 limits new state taxes. It does not change real property taxes or personal property taxes already collected before 2026, such as the business equipment tax counties collect. It does not affect the City's Measure FD or Measure ULA. Its largest effect on this ballot is on Proposition 40: if 42 gets more yes votes, the billionaire tax for health care could be stopped. The Legislative Analyst does not estimate effects on the City of Los Angeles.
The details
Official title Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
What would change
Today If Proposition 42 passes
Taxes on owning personal property The state and local governments tax some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee and the property tax on business equipment paid to counties. Owning financial assets such as stocks and investment accounts is not taxed (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)) No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026 may impose or authorize a tax “on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
What counts as covered property Not applicable Pensions, 401(k), 403(b) and other retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all personal property, tangible or intangible, including financial assets, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property and personal belongings (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Retroactive taxes Allowed in some cases. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)) Barred for taxes based on conduct, activities or a status before the tax took effect, including residency on an earlier date. The Legislature may reach back up to 365 days only for a declared emergency or fiscal emergency, with the money limited to that emergency (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Existing taxes In effect Not affected if in effect and first collected by Dec. 31, 2025 (text, Art. VIII, Secs. 1(b) and 2(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Real property (land and buildings) Taxed under Proposition 13 rules No change (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The measure adds a new Article VIII to the State Constitution. The Legislative Analyst says it “restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future,” which “could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear” (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)).
How it interacts with Proposition 40
Proposition 40 would tax billionaires’ net worth, including businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property, based on residency on Jan. 1, 2026 (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/analysis.htm); official title and summary, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/title-summary.htm)). Proposition 42 bars new taxes on owning those assets and taxes based on residency “on a date prior to the effective date of the tax” (text, Art. VIII, Secs. 1 and 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
The Legislative Analyst: “If Proposition 42 receives more ‘yes’ votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters” (printable guide, Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42.pdf)).
Proposition 42’s conflict clause: a measure on the same ballot that taxes ownership of the covered property, or taxes past conduct or status, is “deemed to be in conflict.” If 42 gets more yes votes, “all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void” (text, Sec. 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Proposition 40’s conflict clause: if 40 gets more yes votes than a measure that affects a tax on billionaire net worth, 40’s provisions prevail (text of Proposition 40, Sec. 8 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
The State Constitution: when measures approved at the same election conflict, the one with the most yes votes prevails (Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Tax attorney Megan Jones of Holland & Knight told CalMatters that “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal” than Proposition 41, and that if it passes it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again (LAist via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/prop-40-the-billionaire-tax-could-be-defeated-by-two-other-tax-measures/ar-AA2cUG36)). Proposition 41 is a second measure that could stop Proposition 40 (our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41)). See also our Proposition 40 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-40).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City and County taxes now. Existing local personal property taxes, such as the property tax on business equipment paid to the County, were in effect before 2026 and are not changed (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm); text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Real property taxes and the City’s Measure ULA transfer tax on real estate sales are outside the measure (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Measure FD, a sales tax, is not a tax on owning property.
Future local taxes. The text bars any “state law” enacted from 2026 on that would “authorize collection” of a tax on owning personal property (text, Art. VIII, Sec. 1(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). The Attorney General’s summary says it “Prohibits new state taxes on personal property” (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/title-summary.htm)). The Legislative Analyst’s fiscal estimate covers the state’s options to raise taxes and does not discuss new local taxes (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 40 money. Proposition 40 would send 90% of its revenue to health care, mostly state programs such as Medi-Cal (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/analysis.htm)). If Proposition 42 stops it, that money would not be collected. Neither analysis estimates what would reach Los Angeles.
Local money from the Yes campaign. The Yes on 42 committee gave $50,000 on April 13, 2026 to the committee backing the City’s Measure FD, and $10,000 on May 5 to the Los Angeles County Democratic Party’s state candidate committee (Cal-Access, committee 1488418 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1488418); our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd)).

Proposition 42 is a citizen initiative, number 2018 on the Secretary of State’s list (Attorney General file 25-0041A1). The proponent is Kurt R.
